headline: Salmon Are Thriving After Klamath River Dam Removals
meta_description: New study shows salmon populations rebounding after dam removals on the Klamath River, with rapid return to breeding grounds triggering ecosystem revival.
summary_short: A new study confirms salmon are thriving following dam removals on the Klamath River, with fish quickly returning to historic breeding grounds.
body:
Salmon are bouncing back after old hydroelectric dams came down on the Klamath River, according to a recent study. The removal of these outdated structures has opened pathways that salmon navigate with surprising speed, rushing into breeding grounds they had been blocked from for decades.

This pattern echoes success seen elsewhere. When dams were removed from the Elwha River, salmon similarly recolonized their ancestral spawning areas rapidly, setting off a cascade of positive changes through the broader ecosystem.

While hydroelectric dams remain valuable for modern power generation, particularly as a relatively sustainable option compared to fossil fuels, aging or inefficient installations can be replaced with newer infrastructure. These removals demonstrate that undoing old barriers isn't just about freeing a single species—it triggers ecosystem revitalization that ripples far beyond the river itself.
quick_facts: Salmon rapidly return to breeding grounds after dam removal
Klamath River dams have been removed in recent project
Similar success observed previously on Elwha River
Ecosystem-wide revival effects follow dam removals
